decisions.quote: Replication of “Walking on eggshells: How expressing relationship insecurities perpetuates them” by EP Lemay, MS Clark (2008, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology). Erica Baranski ericanbaranski@gmail.com Introduction In their original paper, “Walking on eggshells: How expressing relationship insecurities perpetuates them,” Lemay & Clark (2008) tested a model to address unfounded persistent relationship insecurity. Their model of expression-based authenticity doubts suggests that articulating vulnerability ultimately exacerbates one’s own cognitions regarding the insecurity. In other words, being aware that one has expressed vulnerability to rejection results in reflected appraisals of vulnerability, or unrealistic beliefs that the other now views the self as particularly vulnerable. This can, in turn, result in one’s belief that their loved one’s expressions of happiness and affirmation are less genuine. To test the model, they experimentally manipulated participants to monitor the effects of reflected appraisals of vulnerability. In this replication of Lemay & Clark (2008), we sought to exactly reproduce the methodology used in the original paper. As the present work was conducted as part of the Reproducibility Project: Psychology, which asks volunteers to replicate the final study in their chosen paper, this is a direct replication of Experiment 5.

decisions.quote: Discussion We performed a close replication of Experiment 2 by Mitchell and colleagues (2008) and partially replicated their results. We find a similar main effect of same versus different trials, but no main effect of training condition (AX/BX versus CX). Instead, our data provided a tentative indication of an interaction between trial type and condition, with the benefit of intermixed presentation being present for performance on different trials, but not on same trials.
decisions.location: Primary Project Report (https://osf.io/download/beckg/, Daniël Lakens), Discussion, chunk 233 (line 238)
decisions.reason: Input row 1675 (paired with blind target_index 4) evaluates the direct replication of Experiment 2 of Mitchell, Nash, & Hall (2008, JEPLMC, 34(1), 237-242, DOI 10.1037/0278-7393.34.1.237) by Daniël Lakens (N = 48). Shipped coded 'failed' based on the pooled master table's binary 'Replicate (R) = no' indicator for the omnibus main effect of training condition across both same and different trials (F(1, 47) = 0.87, p = .335). However, in the individual primary replication report, the replication author explicitly concludes in the Discussion that 'We performed a close replication of Experiment 2 by Mitchell and colleagues (2008) and partially replicated their results,' finding the main effect of trial type (F(1, 47) = 181.95, p < .001) and a statistically significant intermixed-blocked advantage on the theoretically critical different trials (t(47) = 2.15, p = 0.037, dav = 0.43, with overlapping 95% CIs relative to the original effect), but no effect on same trials (t(47) = 0.33, p = 0.743) and no omnibus main effect across trial types. Under the codebook's hierarchy of evidence (Rule 1), the replication author's explicit overall verdict ('partially replicated their results') governs, making blind's coding ('mixed') right.

decisions.quote: This pattern of findings was replicated in the present study. In agreement with previous findings (Jones & Macken, 1995; Larsen et al., 2000; LeCompte & Shaibe, 1997; Marsh et al., 2008) showing that between-stream phonological similarity does not affect serial recall, between-stream phonological similarity had no effect on performance in the serial recall task, but free recall was more disrupted by phonologically similar distractors in comparison to phonologically dissimilar distractors. However, in contrast to the original study, the critical interaction between instruction type (free recall, serial recall) and sound condition (quiet, phonologically dissimilar, phonologically similar) was not significant. A supplementary analysis confirmed Marsh et al.’s finding that between-stream phonological similarity leads to intrusions errors in free recall. In the present study, phonologically similar speech led to more related-item intrusions in serial recall, too, suggesting that serial recall performance is not completely immune to the effects of between-stream phonological similarity (see Eagan & Chein, 2012, for a similar finding).
decisions.location: Primary Project Report (https://osf.io/download/sqcwk/, Raoul Bell), Discussion, chunks 528-529 (lines 533-534)
decisions.reason: Input row 1676 (paired with blind target_index 10) evaluates the direct replication of Marsh, Vachon, & Jones (2008, JEPLMC, 34(1), 243-248, DOI 10.1037/0278-7393.34.1.243) by Raoul Bell (N = 118). Shipped coded 'failed' based on the pooled master table's binary 'Replicate (R) = no' entry for the 2x3 omnibus interaction (F(2, 232) = 1.63, p = .20). However, in the primary replication report's Results and Discussion, the replication author explicitly concludes that key findings of the original study were replicated—specifically, phonologically similar distractors significantly disrupted free recall compared to dissimilar distractors (t(58) = 4.42, p < .001, partial eta^2 = .25) while having no significant effect on serial recall performance (t(58) = 1.35, p = .18), and the supplementary analysis confirmed the original interaction showing phonological similarity intrusion errors in free recall (F(2, 116) = 15.28, p < .001)—whereas the omnibus 2x3 interaction between instruction type and sound condition was not significant and intrusions also occurred in serial recall. Under the codebook's outcome rules, replicating key focal effects while failing to reach significance on the omnibus interaction constitutes a 'mixed' outcome, making blind's coding ('mixed') right.
